Presidents
PREZ-i-dents
noun (plural)
From the Latin praesidens, present participle of praesidere, “to sit before, to preside over” (prae, before + sedere, to sit); the Authorized Version’s rendering of the Aramaic sarekin, the three chief officers over Darius’s hundred and twenty princes.

Biblical Definition

In the Authorized Version the word belongs to one chapter. Darius set a hundred and twenty princes over his kingdom, “and over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first” (Dan 6:2), that the princes might give accounts to them and the king have no damage. The office is civil, administrative, and pagan — an audit against corruption in a heathen empire — and a believing Jew held the first place in it. That is the first lesson: Daniel served Babylon and then Persia with such diligence that his enemies could find no occasion against him “concerning the kingdom” (Dan 6:4). His faithfulness to God made him the better servant of the state, not the worse. The second lesson follows immediately. Unable to fault his administration, the presidents and princes contrived a law that made prayer to God a capital crime and carried it to the king by flattery (Dan 6:7). Daniel did not organize resistance, did not revile the king, did not flee; he went into his house, opened his windows toward Jerusalem, and prayed as he did aforetime. He then bore the sentence. Here is the whole Christian doctrine of the magistrate in one man: honour the powers that be as ordained of God, obey them in everything lawful, and when they command what God forbids, disobey openly and suffer quietly, for we ought to obey God rather than men.

Webster 1828 Definition

Officers who preside; in Scripture, the three chief ministers over Darius’s princes, of whom Daniel was first.

expand to see more

PRESIDENT, one who is elected or appointed to preside over a body of men, and to direct their proceedings.

From the Latin praesidens, sitting before or over; prae, before, and sedere, to sit.

An officer set over others to receive their accounts and to guard the interest of the sovereign.

In Scripture, the three set over the hundred and twenty princes of the Persian realm (Dan 6:2).

Also, in later use, the chief magistrate of a republic or the head of a corporation.

Key Scripture

Dan 6:2 — "And over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first: that the princes might give accounts unto them, and the king should have no damage."

Dan 6:3 — "Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm."

Dan 6:4 — "Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him."

Dan 6:7 — "All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions."

Modern Corruption

Romans 13 is distorted in two directions at once — a contempt for lawful authority that makes every ordinance of man optional, and a statolatry that hands the magistrate the conscience which belongs to Christ alone.

expand to see more

The first distortion treats civil authority as a nuisance to be evaded wherever it can be evaded, and reads every inconvenient law as tyranny. Scripture does not permit it. The powers that be are ordained of God; the magistrate is His minister, a terror not to good works but to the evil; and the Christian is to be subject not only for wrath but for conscience sake, paying tribute, custom, fear, and honour where each is due. Daniel gave Darius an administration so clean that a hostile audit found nothing. The second distortion is graver because it wears the language of obedience: it takes Rom 13 to mean that whatever the magistrate commands, the Christian must do, and so grants to the state a jurisdiction over the conscience that God has reserved to Himself. The 1689 Confession is exact here — God alone is Lord of the conscience, and to obey men against His word is to betray liberty of conscience and right reason. The decree of Dan 6 was perfectly lawful by Persian process, sealed by the king, unalterable by the law of the Medes and Persians, and utterly void before God the moment it forbade prayer.

Recover the limit and the manner together, for men usually lose one in seizing the other. The limit is Act 5:29 — “We ought to obey God rather than men” — and it is not a general licence to disobey what we dislike but a narrow and absolute refusal at the point where obedience to man requires sin against God. The manner is Daniel’s: no conspiracy, no contempt, no lie, no attempt to escape the penalty. He opened his windows and prayed where he could be seen, and then went down into the den without railing at the king who sent him there. That is Christian civil courage — open in the duty, submissive under the punishment, and content to leave the vindication with God, who shut the lions’ mouths and made a pagan emperor publish His name throughout all the earth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic sarekin, chief officers, likely from an Old Persian root for “head”; Latin praesidere, to sit before — the presiding officer who receives account from those beneath him.

expand to see more

Aramaic — sarekin (סרכין), chief ministers, Dan 6:2; a Persian loanword in the Aramaic of Daniel.

Persian — the underlying sense is one set at the head, an overseer of satraps in the imperial administration.

Latin — praesidere, to sit before or preside; whence praesidens and the English president.

Related — princes in Dan 6 renders achashdarpenayya, the satraps, the hundred and twenty under the three.

Sense — the office is one of audit and account, which is why an incorruptible man was hated in it.

Usage

"“Daniel was first of the three presidents, and his enemies could find no fault in the accounts.”"

"“The decree was lawful by Persian process and void before God the moment it forbade prayer.”"

"“Open in the duty, submissive under the penalty — that is the Daniel pattern for a Christian under an unjust statute.”"
